chapter.title: The Request/Response Model
chapter.para: The chapter showed rexxlets that work without explaining why. This chapter describes the three objects RexxHTTP builds for each request, the buffering underneath the response, and the commit, the single point at which the buffered headers and body are written out. The behaviour a rexxlet author is most likely to find unexpected follows from this model: a header that still takes effect after it appears too late to set, and a header assignment that raises.

section.title: The Three Objects
section.para: For each request, before the rexxlet runs, RexxHTTP builds three objects and hands the rexxlet the first two.

A request (HTTP.Request) is the incoming side, read-only. It holds the request line and headers, reached as named accessors or, for anything CGI passed as an environment variable, through the environment pool. It also holds the arguments and cookies the client sent, parsed and decoded. By the time the rexxlet runs, the parsing is already done and the argument policy already applied, so the request a rexxlet sees is always well-formed.

A response (HTTP.Response) is the outgoing side. It has three parts: a set of headers, seeded with one (Content-Type: text/plain; charset=utf-8), an optional set of cookies, and a buffered output stream that collects the body. The headers and cookies remain modifiable for as long as the body is being written, and are serialised only once, at commit.

An output stream (HTTP.OutputStream) is that body buffer: a write-only subclass of Stream that the response creates for itself. While the rexxlet runs, the default output stream is redirected to it, so a plain SAY writes to the response body. A rexxlet seldom refers to this object by name, and uses SAY instead.

The request and response reach the rexxlet as the environment symbols .request and .response, placed there by the processor. Being environment symbols, they reach the two objects from any scope, including a routine or a method, without the object being passed in. The body of a rexxlet therefore does not have to pass response through every call that might set a header.

section.title: Buffering, and Why
section.para: A CGI program communicates with the web server through its standard output: the bytes it writes become the HTTP response, headers first, then a blank line, then the body. Order is therefore constrained. Once a single header byte has been written, the headers are decided; anything the program sets after that is too late, because it has already been sent. If the body has been sent as well, the header lands in the middle of it.

RexxHTTP avoids this constraint by not writing the body directly to the server. The output stream collects it in a buffer. While the buffer fills, the headers and cookies are entries in two directories on the response object. Setting one, changing one and adding a cookie are ordinary updates to in-memory state, and the order in which the rexxlet performs them relative to its SAY instructions does not matter, because none of it has been serialised yet.

This is what the introduction and the chapter called lazy headers. A rexxlet can write half its page, determine from what it computed there that the content type should be text/html rather than the default, set it, and finish the page. The header is correct on the wire, because nothing had been committed at the point where it was set. The buffer is what allows the rexxlet to decide late.

section.title: Commit
section.para: Commit is the point at which the buffered head is written out. It happens once per response, and performs a fixed sequence: it writes the Content-Type header, then one Set-Cookie line per scheduled cookie, then every other header, then the blank line that separates head from body. All of this goes directly to the server's output stream, ahead of the buffered body. After commit the head has been sent and cannot be changed.

Commit is idempotent: the first call emits the head and marks the response committed; any later call returns immediately, having done nothing. A rexxlet therefore does not have to track whether the response is already committed before requesting a flush. Requesting one twice has no effect.

Rexxlets seldom call commit directly. It is driven by flush. The response's flush (and the output stream's, which it delegates to) commits the response if it has not been committed yet, and only then writes the buffered body out and empties the buffer. The first flush is what commits, and that first flush is one of two things:

listitem.para: one the rexxlet performs itself, by calling .response~flush, for instance to fix the headers at a chosen point; or
the one RexxHTTP performs automatically after the rexxlet returns.

section.para: A rexxlet that never flushes still receives exactly one flush, the processor's final one, and so still produces a complete response with its head committed once. The common case requires no flush at all.

section.title: Commit Discipline
section.para: Everything a rexxlet can do to the head is legal before commit and an error after it. This covers setting a header (.response[...]= or the message form), scheduling a cookie (addcookie), and replacing the response wholesale (error, 404, redirect). Past commit the head has already been sent, so a late change could not take effect. RexxHTTP treats the attempt as a programming error and raises (Syntax 93.900, the response is already committed) rather than accept a call it would have to ignore silently. The body may still be written and flushed after commit; only the head is frozen.

The order of the guards therefore matters in one place. When a cookie is added to an already-committed response, the failure reported is already committed, not not a cookie, even if the argument is also wrong: the commit check comes first, because the commit state takes precedence over argument validation. The same order governs error and redirect, which discard an uncommitted buffered body and do their work, but raise on a committed response rather than appearing to change a status that has already been sent.

There is also a brief internal window that the rexxlet does not observe. While commit is partway through writing the head, the response is committing but not yet committed. RexxHTTP's own error handling distinguishes the two, so that a fault raised while headers are being emitted does not attempt to re-assert headers over a response that is already half-written. A rexxlet only ever observes the two stable states, before and after; committed reports which. section.title: A Note on Streaming and mod_deflate
section.para: The ability to flush early does not mean that a rexxlet can stream a page to the browser progressively, a piece at a time. The 2006 manual made approximately that promise. In a modern production deployment it does not hold.

The reason is mod_deflate. To compress the response, Apache's mod_deflate buffers the CGI program's output on its own account before sending it on, so the boundaries at which a rexxlet flushes are not the boundaries at which the client receives anything; the compressor determines those. An early .response~flush does not reliably make the first half of a page appear in the browser before the rexxlet has finished computing the second half.

What an early flush does do is internal, and is the reason the flush mechanism is kept. It commits the response at a chosen point, fixing the headers and status there rather than at the end. That control over commit ordering is occasionally what a rexxlet requires, and it is the mechanism behind the lazy-header behaviour described above. flush means decide the head now, not send bytes to the browser now. For most rexxlets neither concern arises: they write their body, return, and let the processor's final flush commit and send the whole response at once.
